title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Corpse in the Thames: The Novel's Dark Bargain

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be working through the whole strange, brilliant, unnerving thing — from the body in the Thames to the dust heaps to the mercenary drawing rooms of London.
This first episode begins where the novel begins — on the river, at night, with a man fishing for corpses.
To help us think about what Dickens is doing from the very first page, I'm joined by three extraordinary guests.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he brings a fierce, precise eye to the question of who the system produces as its waste.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what the Thames riverbed meant in 1865 — as an economic zone, a legal space, a site of both livelihood and horror.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than any living person — brings us the novel as a performance, as a thing made of rhythm and voice and timing.
Welcome, all three of you.
Daniel, let's start with you — because the opening of this novel is, I think, one of the most calculated opening gambits in all of Victorian fiction.
It really is — and I think we have to be clear about what the calculation is.
Dickens opens this novel with Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie, rowing on the Thames at night, towing a dead body behind their boat.
And the very first thing Gaffer says — when Lizzie looks away from the water — is that she has no right to be squeamish.
He tells her this is how they eat, how they live — the river feeds them.
So before we've even turned the first page, Dickens has established the central brutal bargain of the novel: survival requires complicity with death.
And crucially, this is not framed as a moral failing on Gaffer's part — it's framed as the condition the poor are placed in.
The system creates this economy out of corpses, and then holds the poor in contempt for participating in it.
And the historical reality is even darker than the fiction, which is saying something.
The Thames dredgers and bodyfinders were a recognised, if deeply marginal, occupation in mid-Victorian London.
Henry Mayhew documented them — they were called 'dredgermen,' and they worked on a kind of grim commission: found property, including bodies, entitled them to a reward.
The law was quite specific: a finder had certain rights over recovered property, which is why Gaffer's livelihood has a legal dimension as well as a moral one.
Dickens understood this perfectly — which is why the Veneering dinner party in the very next chapter feels like a different planet.
The wealth circulating in those drawing rooms is no less built on death — it's just that nobody names the body.
James has put his finger on exactly what makes that structural juxtaposition so devastating as a piece of storytelling.
Chapter one: the river, the dark, a dead man being towed through the water.
Chapter two: glittering dinner party, the newly rich Veneerings, everybody performing wealth they haven't quite earned yet.
Dickens doesn't comment on the connection — he simply places them side by side and trusts you.
That is great novelistic confidence — the kind that comes from a writer at the absolute height of his craft.
And that opening sentence — 'In these times of ours, though concerning the exact year there is no need to be precise' — is doing something very interesting with time.
'In these times of ours, though concerning the exact year there is no need to be precise.'
It's a narrator who refuses to pin the story down — as if to say: this is not history, this is now, this is always.
That point about time is sharper than it might first appear.
'These times of ours' — it's a gesture toward the universal, yes, but it's also an indictment of the present tense.
Dickens is writing in 1864 and 1865, the height of speculative capitalism in England — the era of the railway swindle, the fraudulent joint-stock company.
The Veneerings and their kind are a direct satirical portrait of that moment — people who have purchased the appearance of old money.
And Dickens shows you the corpse first — before the dinner party — so that you understand what funds the dinner.
The Harmon will is the engine of this, of course — and it's worth pausing on just how grotesque that inheritance plot actually is.
Old John Harmon has made his fortune from dust — from the sorting and selling of London's refuse.
And his will stipulates that his son can only inherit if he marries a woman his father has selected for him — a woman the son has never met.
This is not sentimental Victorian plotting — this is property law weaponised as posthumous control.
The dead man's hand reaches from the grave and arranges a marriage market — and then a body turns up in the Thames that may or may not be the heir.
What I love — and I use that word with full awareness — is that Dickens gives us all of this in the first three chapters without once losing his comic nerve.
The Veneering dinner party is one of the funniest set pieces in the whole novel — possibly in all of Dickens.
The Analytical Chemist — the Veneerings' butler — who goes around the table with a face of permanent existential reproach.
Dickens describes him as always seeming to say, 'I give it up' — as if civilisation itself has failed and he alone has noticed.
The comedy is dark, but it is comedy — and Dickens knows that darkness needs laughter the way a fire needs air.
Strip out the jokes and you don't have a darker novel — you have a lesser one.
That tension — between the comic and the catastrophic — is something we'll be returning to throughout this series.
But I want to stay with Gaffer Hexam for a moment — because he's such a strange figure to open with.
He's not sympathetic in any comfortable sense — he's fierce, he's controlling, he has a violent contempt for what he calls sneaking.
And yet the novel asks us to see the system that made him — Daniel, is that a fair reading?
Absolutely fair — and I'd push it further.
Gaffer's contempt for sneaking — meaning theft from the living, as opposed to his own trade — is a code of honour that the system has forced him to construct.
He draws a moral line in the water, so to speak — because without some line, there is nothing left of him as a person.
And Rogue Riderhood — his former partner — is the shadow version of Gaffer: the man who has crossed that line.
Dickens uses their relationship to show us what the moral economy of the very poor actually looks like from the inside — with its own distinctions, its own sense of dignity.
That is a radically empathetic act for a novelist writing for a middle-class audience in the 1860s.
Riderhood is also a beautifully precise legal creation, incidentally.
He is the kind of man who lives at the edges of criminality without ever quite being prosecutable — always available for perjury, for false witness, for information sold to the highest bidder.
The Victorian legal system created men like Riderhood — it needed them, as informers, as runners, as tools.
And then it held them in utter contempt — which is exactly how the novel presents him.
Riderhood nearly drowning — and then being dragged back to life — is one of the strangest and most powerful passages in the novel.
Dickens writes that as Riderhood begins to return to consciousness, the people around him — who despise him utterly — find themselves willing him back.
Because life is life — even in a worthless man, it's worth preserving.
And then the moment he is clearly going to live, they lose interest — and their contempt returns like a tide.
That is not satire — that is something much more unsettling.
The river gives and the river takes away — and the novel never quite lets you be comfortable about which is which.
In our next segment, we'll be diving into the dust heaps — the other great source of fortune in this novel — and asking what Dickens means by making garbage the engine of an inheritance plot.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Money, Dust, and the Making of the Poor

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, scene by scene, to see what's working beneath the surface.
I'm your host, and today we're beginning with the novel's great foundational obsession: money, dust, and what the system does to the people at the bottom of it.
With me are three guests who bring very different kinds of attention to this extraordinary book.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and in Our Mutual Friend, he has found one of the richest specimens in all of Victorian fiction.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows what the institutions Dickens depicts actually were, and what it cost a human being to pass through them.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has narrated more classic novels than perhaps any living voice — he hears the rhythms and the comedy and the silence that other readers miss.
Let's begin at the beginning — with a dead man in the river and a fortune made of rubbish.
What Dickens establishes in the very opening pages is an economy — not a story, not a mystery, an economy.
The Thames is not a picturesque backdrop. It's a labour market.
Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie are out on the river in the darkness, harvesting corpses for whatever coin they can find on the bodies.
Dickens describes Gaffer's boat as if it is a kind of predatory creature — and the man himself as utterly without sentiment about the work.
He says of Gaffer, in that first chapter, something to the effect that he had no personal feeling in the matter — he was used to it.
And that phrase — 'used to it' — is the novel's first great indictment.
A man has been so thoroughly shaped by economic necessity that death has become routine labour. That is what poverty manufactures.
And it's worth being precise about what that labour actually was, historically.
River-finders — mudlarks, in the broader category — were a documented and legally ambiguous class of worker in mid-Victorian London.
Recovering a drowned body entitled you to a coroner's fee — a modest one — plus whatever was on the person.
The law was not clear on how much of what you found you could keep, and the law being unclear was, as ever, to the disadvantage of the poor.

Dickens understood this precisely. Gaffer's pride — his insistence that he is not a common thief, that he never robs the dead — is the pride of a man desperately policing the one moral distinction left to him.
When he says, in effect, that what's found in the clothes of a drowned man is the lawful finder's due, he is articulating a customary right the law did not reliably honour.
What I find astonishing, reading it aloud, is how Dickens manages to make Gaffer simultaneously repellent and entirely sympathetic within about four paragraphs.
The prose does something very specific: it refuses to let you settle into a comfortable response.
Lizzie — his daughter — is rowing in the opening scene, and she keeps her face turned away from whatever it is her father is pulling toward the boat.
That detail is everything. She knows. She participates. She cannot bear to look.
Dickens writes that her face has a listening expression — as if she's hearing something dreadful approach rather than seeing it.
That phrase — 'a listening expression' — is the kind of thing that stops you cold when you're reading for voice.
It's doing the work of an entire psychology in three words.
But let's move up the river, economically speaking — to the dust mounds, which are the novel's central image of how wealth is actually produced.
Old Harmon — the elder Harmon, the father — has made an enormous fortune from what the novel consistently calls dust.
Dust, in the mid-Victorian period, meant something specific: household refuse, ash, cinders — the accumulated waste of London's domestic life.
It was sorted and sold — cinders for brick-making, rags for paper, bones for fertiliser — and the men who controlled the great dust-yards grew very rich indeed.
Dickens is absolutely deliberate in this choice of foundation for the Harmon fortune.
All wealth, the image insists, is the transformation of refuse — the labour of the invisible poor — into capital that enriches those who merely own the yard.
The dust contractors were genuinely wealthy. Henry Dodd of Islington — often cited as one of Dickens's models for old Harmon — left a very substantial estate.
The industry was unregulated, the labour of the sorters was brutal, and the margins at the top were extraordinary.
What Dickens also understood — and this is the sharp satirical point — is that the English middle class was perfectly comfortable accepting money whose origins they preferred not to examine.
The Veneerings are the novel's great image of this. New money laundered into social respectability so fast you can barely track the transformation.
Dickens says everything in the Veneering household is new — the house, the furniture, the carriage, the plate, the servant.

'All their furniture was new, all their friends were new, all their servants were new, their plate was new, their carriage was new, their harness was new, their horses were new, their pictures were new.'
The repetition is merciless — and the comedy is absolutely devastating.
The Veneering chapters are one of the great set-pieces of English satire — I would put them alongside anything in Thackeray, which is saying something.

The device of Twemlow — this bewildered, gentle, minor aristocrat who keeps appearing at Veneering dinner parties and can never quite work out what his relationship to his host actually is — is a masterpiece of comic construction.
Dickens describes him as the oldest friend of the Veneerings — which is a distinction that dates back, he notes with perfect timing, all of five weeks.
But what gives the satire its weight — and this is what distinguishes Dickens from mere comedy — is that the Veneerings are not the villains.
They are the system made flesh. They are what money aspires to when it has no other ambition than to be seen.
And against all of this — the dust fortunes, the Veneering glitter — Dickens places the figure of Betty Higden.
Betty Higden is an old woman who minds children for a living and is utterly, absolutely, terrified of one thing above all others: the workhouse.
She is not a comic figure. She is Dickens at his most nakedly political.
She says — and I want to get this right because the words matter — that she would far rather die on the road than be taken into the parish.
'Disgraced and done-for she would be if she went into the workhouse, which she'd far rather die than do.'
That fear is not irrational. The workhouse was designed to be feared. That was its mechanism of social control.
And she dies, in the end, on the road — having walked herself to exhaustion rather than submit. Dickens makes her die free. That is his rage made visible.
The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act is the legislation behind Betty Higden's terror.

It replaced outdoor relief — money paid to the poor in their own homes — with the principle of less eligibility: the condition of the pauper must be less comfortable than that of the lowest independent labourer.
In practice, this meant families separated, uniforms worn, diets calibrated to the edge of subsistence. Deliberately punitive. As policy.
Our Mutual Friend was published in 1864-65. Thirty years after the Act, and Dickens is still furious — because the system had not changed, and the fear had not changed.
Betty Higden is, among other things, Dickens's direct reply to those who defended the workhouse as philanthropy.
There's a preface to this novel — Dickens wrote it after Betty Higden's story provoked exactly the kind of comfortable outrage he was anticipating.
People wrote to him to say that surely the workhouse was not so bad — that the fear he depicted was exaggerated.
And Dickens is — if you'll allow the word — magnificent in his response.
He essentially says: I have investigated. I have been to these places. I know what I wrote.
The tone of that postscript is very cold. Dickens angry and certain is not a comfortable thing to read.
There's a third strand I want to bring into this — because we've talked about the bottom and the dazzling top, but the novel's most interesting territory is the anxious middle.
Silas Wegg. Mr. Venus. Fascination Fledgeby. These are people who have partially escaped poverty and are absolutely determined not to go back.
Wegg's plot against Boffin — the attempt to use the discovered will as blackmail — is not really about greed in the normal sense.
It's about the terror of someone who has glimpsed, from a ballad-seller's stall in the street, what wealth looks like — and cannot bear to be outside it.
Dickens gives Wegg a missing leg — which he keeps, in pieces, at Mr. Venus's shop — and that image is absolutely right.
He is a man whose very body has been taken from him by economic hardship and sold piecemeal. His revenge fantasy is just his body trying to reassemble itself.
And Mr. Venus — the articulator of human skeletons — is one of the great comic grotesques of Victorian fiction.
He sits in his shop surrounded by preserved specimens — 'human warious,' as Dickens has him say — in a state of total romantic despair.
The woman he loves has rejected him because she objects, she says, to being 'regarded in that boney light.'
'I do not wish to be regarded in that boney light.'
It is one of the greatest comic refusals in all of Dickens. The timing, the vocabulary, the pathos — all of it perfect.
But even Mr. Venus — even this apparently absurdist figure — is doing a real trade in a real Victorian market, which James knows better than I do.
The trade in human bones and specimens was entirely real and entirely legal.
Medical schools needed skeletons. Artists needed anatomical models. There was a market, and there were people who served it.
What Dickens understands — and what gives Venus his peculiar dignity — is that the man is a craftsman.
Articulating a skeleton — putting the joints and connections precisely right — requires real skill and real knowledge.
Venus is proud of his work. He objects to Wegg on moral grounds, ultimately — there is a line he will not cross.
Dickens locates genuine ethical integrity in the most apparently grotesque corners of his novel. It's never where you expect it.
That seems to me the essential truth of this novel's economy — moral value is always inverted from monetary value.
The people with the least money have, again and again, the most dignity.
We're going to come back to what money does to the people who actually inherit it — to John Harmon, to the Boffins, and to the extraordinary trap Bella Wilfer finds herself in.
But first, a short break. Don't go anywhere.

segments.title: The Comic Grotesques: Podsnappery and Performance

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time this episode in some of the novel's darker corridors — the dust heaps, the river, the grinding machinery of poverty.
Now we turn to something that is, on the surface, considerably more festive — and underneath, just as merciless.
We're talking about Podsnap, and the whole glittering, suffocating world of Podsnappery.
Oliver, you have lived inside more Dickens performances than anyone at this table — where does Podsnap sit for you among the great comic grotesques?
Right at the top, I'd say — and I don't mean that lightly.
Dickens has given us brilliant comic monsters before, but Podsnap is different because he's not merely ridiculous — he is the establishment, perfectly rendered.
There's that extraordinary passage in the second chapter of Book One where Dickens essentially invents the word — 'Podsnappery' — as a social diagnosis.
He describes Podsnap's world as one in which everything inconvenient or uncomfortable can simply be swept away with a wave of the hand.
"I don't want to know about it; I don't choose to discuss it; I don't admit it!"
That gesture — the famous Podsnap sweep — is one of the great physical comic inventions in English fiction.
And what's terrifying is how recognisable it still is.
And Dickens is precise about what that gesture protects.
Podsnap isn't sweeping away abstract unpleasantness — he's sweeping away the poor, the foreign, the morally inconvenient.
Dickens makes this explicit when he introduces him — Podsnap has made a 'good thing' of the marine insurance business, and he has translated commercial success into a complete moral cosmology.
The system rewards him, so the system must be right, so anyone the system crushes must have deserved crushing.
That's not satire of an individual eccentric — that is an anatomy of ideology.
And the historical specificity is worth attending to here.
Marine insurance in the 1860s was one of the great pillars of City wealth — respectable, opaque, deeply connected to imperial trade.
Dickens is very deliberate in choosing that profession for Podsnap rather than, say, manufacturing or retail.
It places him at a remove from actual production — he profits from the movement of goods without ever touching them.
Which is, as Daniel says, the perfect economic foundation for a man who refuses to acknowledge the material reality of anything inconvenient.
But then there's the dinner party — which is where Podsnap becomes genuinely, uncomfortably funny.
Dickens stages the whole scene as a kind of ritual humiliation of a foreign guest — the unfortunate 'foreign gentleman' who cannot make Podsnap understand anything outside England.
Podsnap speaks to him in a bellowing, simplified English, as though volume could substitute for comprehension.
And there's that glorious exchange where Podsnap insists that English institutions are the finest in the world and demands the foreigner confirm it.
"We Englishmen are Very Proud of our Constitution, Sir. It Was Bestowed Upon Us By Providence."
The capital letters are almost audible when you read that aloud — it's written for performance.
Dickens is parodying not just Podsnap but a whole register of public self-congratulation.
What I want to add to Oliver's reading is that the foreigner in that scene functions as a kind of mirror.
His incomprehension is genuine — he cannot parse Podsnap's assumptions because those assumptions are not universal, they are class-specific and nationally specific.
And Dickens uses that gap — between what Podsnap claims is universal and what the foreigner can actually hear — to expose the parochialism beneath the imperialism.
The funniest moment is when the foreigner asks a perfectly reasonable question about poverty in England, and Podsnap dismisses it with that sweep.
The comedy and the politics are completely fused — you cannot separate them.
There's a counterpart figure worth bringing in here: Veneering.
Where Podsnap is old money pretending to be eternal, Veneering is new money pretending to be old — and Dickens treats them as two faces of the same social performance.
The Veneering dinner table scenes are practically a sociology of mid-Victorian aspiration — everyone performing a relationship to status they have not quite earned.
Dickens describes their furniture and their guests in the same breath — both are acquisitions, both are display.
And the Analytical Chemist — the Veneerings' manservant — who stands in the corner with an expression of permanent, refined disgust, is one of the great silent comic characters in the book.
He knows exactly what this all is, and he cannot say a word.
The Analytical Chemist is a masterpiece of compression.
He never speaks — he communicates entirely through the act of offering wine with an expression suggesting it may be poisoned.
Dickens describes him as one who has 'given up hope of the human race.'
"The Analytical Chemist, a pensive butler who has given up hope of the human race."
Eight words and a whole inner life — that is Dickens at his most economical.
And when you perform it aloud, you realise the joke is also a kind of tenderness — the man sees clearly, and that clarity is its own punishment.
Podsnappery as a system requires constant performance from everyone in its orbit.
Consider Georgiana Podsnap — the daughter, this pale, frightened girl produced by this thunderous household.
She has been so thoroughly shaped by her father's social machinery that she barely knows how to express an honest feeling.
When Lammle and his wife begin to manipulate her toward Fledgeby, she is almost incapable of resisting because she has never been taught that her own desires are legitimate.
The comic grotesque has a victim, and her name is Georgiana, and she is not funny at all.
That's exactly right, and it's where the comedy becomes something more uncomfortable.
Dickens was writing at a moment when a daughter was legally her father's property until marriage, and then her husband's.
Georgiana has no legal personhood to speak of — she exists within Podsnap's domestic empire precisely as his furniture does.
The Married Women's Property Act was still a decade away when this novel was published.
So when Dickens shows her as a terrified, infantilised figure produced by a father who sweeps inconvenient reality aside — he is also describing a legal reality.
And there's a very specific moment I think of when Dickens describes Mrs. Podsnap — with those 'rocking-horse nostrils' — as a kind of auxiliary enforcer of the system.
She is just as suffocating as her husband, in her own way — perhaps more so because she does it with a kind of formidable social competence.
Dickens gives her that extraordinary physical description early in the book — she has 'a quantity of bone, neck and nostrils.'
"Mrs Veneering was a young woman with rather large bones, fair complexion, and quiet eyes."
Actually, forgive me — the bone-and-nostrils line is Mrs. Podsnap herself.
The point is that these women are rendered with the same objectifying eye that their husbands bring to everything — which is Dickens's darkest joke.
There's something almost theatrical about the whole Podsnap section of the novel — a staged world where the staging is itself the subject.
Daniel, you've argued that the comedy here isn't a relief from the novel's serious concerns — it is the serious concern.
Can you close out this thread by saying something about what Podsnap costs the novel — or gives it?
What Podsnap gives the novel is a name for the thing the whole novel is fighting against.
Every time a character in Our Mutual Friend is ignored, or dismissed, or denied their full humanity — that is Podsnappery at work, even when Podsnap is not in the room.
Gaffer Hexam's death — no one of consequence mourns it.
Betty Higden's terror of the workhouse — officially, that terror doesn't exist; it isn't nice to mention.
Podsnap gave Dickens a verb, almost — to Podsnap something is to refuse to see it.
And the novel is one long, magnificent act of forcing the reader to see anyway.
Beautifully put.
Podsnap as the novel's great diagnostic tool — the figure that makes visible what the system otherwise prefers to keep obscured.

Coming up, we'll look at the novel's strange, layered ending — what Dickens resolves, what he leaves deliberately open, and what the dust heaps and the river ultimately mean for all those who have been living beside them.

segments.title: Bella's Question: Can Money Buy a Self?

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most compelling arcs — the education of Bella Wilfer.
Bella enters the novel as a young woman who is quite openly, quite defiantly, in love with money.
She's bequeathed to a dead man she never met, and she resents the whole absurd arrangement with magnificent frankness.
But Dickens is far too interesting a novelist to leave her there.
So the question we're putting to our panel today is this: can money buy a self — and what does it cost Bella to find out?
With me as always are Dr. Daniel Rosen, cultural historian and our resident anatomist of class power.
Prof. James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who keeps us honest about what the world behind the novel actually looked like.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has given voice to more of these characters than anyone alive.
Daniel, let's start with you — because Bella's attitude to money is so brazen, so unapologetic, that it almost feels like a provocation from Dickens himself.
It is a provocation — and I think it's one of the most radical things Dickens ever wrote.
Because Bella doesn't pretend.
She says directly to her father — this is early in Book Two — that she is mercenary, and she knows it, and she hates herself for it, but she is.
That's Dickens stripping away the polite fiction that Victorian women were above material considerations.
Bella has been made into a commodity — bequeathed, handed around — and she has internalised that logic completely.
She wants money because money is the only power available to her in this system.
That's not a character flaw — that's a structural condition.
Daniel's absolutely right that the honesty is extraordinary — but I want to dwell on the pleasure of it for a moment.
Bella in those early chapters with her father — Rumty Wilfer, dear, ineffectual Rumty — is genuinely funny.
She bullies him with enormous affection and he adores every second of it.
But then Dickens gives her that speech — and it's a speech, it's written for the voice — where she tells her father she wants to be rich.
She says something to the effect that she wants to be something so much better than the best of the people she sees, and that she is always envying and angry.
That word — angry — lands like a stone.
This isn't a girl who wants frocks and jewels — this is someone who is furious at her own powerlessness.
And that powerlessness has a very precise legal and social shape in the 1860s.
Bella's situation — bequeathed to a man who then drowns before the marriage can occur — is a genuine legal curiosity.
She has no claim on the Harmon estate, and yet she is lodged with the Boffins almost as a ward, almost as a dependent.
Her entire social position is defined by a dead man's whim — and the Married Women's Property Act is still years away.
So when Bella says she wants money, she is articulating something absolutely rational given the constraints of her world.
Without it, she is, legally and practically, nothing.
And this is where the Boffin plot becomes so interesting — and so troubling.
Noddy Boffin, the Golden Dustman, begins to perform miserliness — at Rokesmith's instigation — to show Bella what the love of money actually produces.
He becomes cruel to Rokesmith — humiliates him in front of Bella — and Bella's reaction is the hinge of the whole novel.
She is disgusted.
She throws off the wealth and walks out — and this is Dickens's argument: that Bella has a self underneath the mercenary performance, and it reasserts itself when tested.
But I want to be careful here — because Dickens's solution is to marry her to a rich man anyway.
The novel rewards her virtue with precisely the material comfort she wanted all along.
Daniel, you are absolutely determined to deny us a happy ending.
But I think the scene at the Boffins' — when Bella defends Rokesmith against what she believes is genuine cruelty — is genuinely moving.
She doesn't know Rokesmith is Harmon in disguise.
She doesn't know she's being tested.
And yet she chooses moral indignation over a wealthy household — that is the novel's proof of her character.
Dickens writes her walking out with what he calls a blush on her cheek and a light in her eye — and it's one of those moments where you feel the novelist's own pride in his creation.
I want to return to the Boffin stratagem for a moment, because it's been debated almost since the novel was published.
Was it planned from the beginning — Boffin and Rokesmith together engineering Bella's moral education — or did Dickens invent it as he went?
The structural seams are visible — some readers find the revelation that Boffin was performing all along a cheat.
But I think the more interesting point is what it says about female education in this period.
Bella is being educated — by men, without her knowledge or consent — into a version of herself they have decided is correct.
The question of whether she found her self, or whether her self was manufactured for her, is not one the novel quite confronts.
James has put his finger on something the novel can't fully resolve — and I think it's because Dickens himself can't fully resolve it.
The dust heaps dominate this novel — they are the symbol of wealth accumulated through what other people throw away.
And the inheritance of that wealth is what everyone is fighting over — Wegg, the Boffins, the Wilfers, the whole seething cast.
Bella's arc is meant to show that money can't buy virtue — but it ends with virtue being rewarded by money.
The ideology of the novel and the plot mechanics are pulling in opposite directions.
I want to come to Bella's defence one more time — because there's a scene that I think settles something important.
When Bella and John Rokesmith — still as the secretary — have their conversation by the river, and she is trying to work out what she feels for him —
she tells him she is the most mercenary little wretch that ever lived in the world.
The self-awareness in that line is extraordinary — she is diagnosing herself even as she is falling in love.
That's not a woman whose self has been manufactured for her — that's a woman watching herself change and naming it out loud.
Dickens gives her that language — and it's generous, it's comic, it's true.
I think that phrase — the most mercenary little wretch that ever lived — is one of the great moments of Dickensian comic self-knowledge.
And it raises the question we'll carry into the next section: what does Bella's story look like when set against the other great love plot in this novel — Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam?
Because if Bella's story is about money and self-discovery, theirs is about class, desire, and something far more dangerous.
That's where we're heading — after a short break.

segments.title: Harmon's Purgatory: Identity, Crime, and Resurrection

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the river all morning — the dust mounds, the money, the marriages of convenience.
Now we arrive at what I'd call the novel's most daring structural gamble: John Harmon's false death.
A man inherits a fortune on the condition he marry a woman he's never met — and instead he stages his own disappearance.
He becomes Julius Handford, then John Rokesmith — lodging in the house of the very woman he was supposed to marry.
It's a plot worthy of sensation fiction, and yet Dickens uses it for something far stranger and more philosophical.
With me to unpack all of this: Dr. Daniel Rosen, whose reading of Harmon I suspect will be rather unforgiving of the gentleman.
Prof. James Blackstone, who can tell us precisely what the law made of a man believed dead in 1865.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has read John Rokesmith aloud more than once and knows where the voice cracks.
What fascinates me first and always about the Harmon plot is that extraordinary long soliloquy — really a sustained act of self-interrogation — in Chapter Twelve of the second book.
Harmon sits alone and essentially tries to reconstruct, from fragments of drugged consciousness, whether he himself committed a murder.
It reads unlike anything else in Dickens.
The narrator keeps saying something like: 'I, John Harmon, should be buried with the man in the river' — and then pulling back and saying, but I am not that man.
It has a quality almost of a fever dream — the syntax itself becomes unstable, as though identity might dissolve at the grammatical level.
And Dickens earns it, I think, because the performance question it poses is genuinely hard: at what point does a man playing dead become a new man?
I want to press on something Oliver raises, because I think the 'new man' framing is exactly what the novel wants us to accept — and we should resist it, at least partly.
John Harmon has immense privilege in this plot.
He can afford to be dead.
He has resources, mobility, literacy — he can construct a new identity as a secretary, gain employment in the Wilfer household.
Meanwhile Gaffer Hexam is hauling corpses from the Thames to scrape together a living, and nobody is writing him a soliloquy about the ambiguity of his personhood.
The novel invites us to find Harmon's self-examination profound, and it is — but that profundity is an index of class.
Only certain people get to be philosophically dead.
Daniel's point about privilege is well-taken, and I'd add a strictly legal dimension that darkens it further.
In the 1860s, if you were presumed dead and your estate passed to another party, reclaiming it was extremely difficult — and you could face charges of fraud.
What protects Harmon is that the Boffins know, eventually, and they're complicit.
The entire charade depends on a network of goodwill from people who have no legal obligation to extend it.
And there's an irony the novel sits with quietly: the man who was supposed to inherit old Harmon's money ends up being employed as a secretary in the house that money bought.
He is, in legal terms, a dependent in his own inheritance.
'A dependent in his own inheritance' — James, that's Dickens's joke, isn't it, told in slow motion over about six hundred pages.
And the performance of Rokesmith is crucial because he has to be convincing as a subordinate — meek, efficient, industrious.
There's a moment where Bella Wilfer treats Rokesmith with something close to contempt — she calls him mercenary, she accuses him quite savagely.
And he bears it.
He absorbs the insult, and the reader watches a man who could reveal everything — who holds all the cards — choosing silence.
That's the theatrical engine of the whole disguise plot: the gap between what the audience knows and what Bella knows.
It's extremely uncomfortable dramatic irony, and I think Dickens knew exactly how uncomfortable it was.
Uncomfortable is one word for it.
I'd say it's the novel testing Bella — but also, uncomfortably, testing our sympathy for the man doing the testing.
Because Harmon — Rokesmith — is surveilling Bella.
He is observing her character under false pretenses, deciding whether she is worthy of him and his fortune.
That's a significant power asymmetry — and the novel dresses it up as romantic patience.
Bella has no idea she is being evaluated, the way one evaluates livestock at a fair.
The old Harmon's will — 'marry this woman or lose the lot' — has contaminated the entire courtship, even in disguise.
The will is the mechanism, you're right — and old Harmon's will is itself a spectacular act of posthumous coercion.
Victorian testamentary law gave enormous latitude to wealthy men to control behaviour from beyond the grave.
A conditional bequest of that kind — marry this named person, or forfeit — was entirely enforceable.
What Dickens understood — and dramatises brilliantly — is that the will doesn't die with the testator.

Old Harmon's cruelty — he was, by all accounts in the novel, a deeply unpleasant man who estranged his children — that cruelty gets transcribed into a legal document and continues to deform every relationship in the book.
The dust mounds are a monument to hoarding, and the will is hoarding's extension into eternity.
James's phrase — 'hoarding's extension into eternity' — is exactly the texture of this novel.

And what Dickens does with Harmon's resurrection — and it is, structurally, a resurrection — is to suggest that the only way to escape the father's dead hand is to die and be reborn outside the system.
When Harmon finally reveals himself to the Boffins, and later to Bella, there's a quality of a man stepping back into life after having genuinely audited it.

The great moment in the soliloquy — and I return to it compulsively — is where he says, to put it roughly, that he is glad he took the experience of being nobody, because it showed him what he actually valued.
The purgatory wasn't punishment — it was education.
The river takes you down and gives you back something the money could never have purchased.
I don't want to be the tedious sceptic, but I do want to note: at the end of all that purgatorial education, Harmon gets the money.
He gets the girl, and he gets the fortune.
The system that was supposed to be tested — inheritance, conditional marriage, the commodification of human beings — it's not dismantled; it's redeemed.
And I find that genuinely interesting as a formal problem.
Because the novel is far more radical in its anatomy of what's wrong than in its prescription for what should happen instead.
Dickens sees the rot clearly, and then, at the last moment, asks his hero to redeem it from within.
That's the characteristic Victorian ending, isn't it — not revolution, but renovation.
The Boffins, too, are an instructive case.
Noddy Boffin is a working man who inherits a capitalist's fortune and must decide, in real time, what money does to a person.

And Dickens stages — though not everyone finds this convincing — a performance within a performance, where Boffin's apparent corruption is itself an act, designed to demonstrate to Bella what avarice really looks like.
The architecture of disguise and performance in this novel is vertiginous — Harmon watches Bella, Boffin performs corruption, Riderhood performs information-selling.
Everyone is staging a self for the benefit of an audience who doesn't know they're watching a performance.
As a professional performer, I find the Boffin business almost unbearably rich.
Because Dickens asks Noddy Boffin — this great warm dusty sunflower of a man — to perform something genuinely ugly.
Boffin collects books about misers, he haggles viciously, he humiliates Rokesmith publicly.
And then the reveal — that it was all theatre, all for Bella's moral benefit — it's either a stroke of genius or a piece of authorial wish-fulfilment, depending on where you sit.
I've read it both ways, and I think the novel holds both possibilities open, deliberately.
The real question is whether you believe that moral education through deception is a kindness — and Dickens doesn't quite settle it.
That unsettlement is where I find the novel most honest.
Because the whole question of what Harmon's resurrection means depends on whether we believe in the sincerity of the moral transformation it's supposed to have produced in Bella.
Bella begins the novel as someone who openly desires money and status — Dickens is admirably unsentimental about that.
She is, in her own words, a mercenary little wretch.
'I am the most mercenary little wretch that ever lived in the world.'
And there's something bracing about a Dickens heroine who says that aloud, without waiting to be found out.
What the novel then tries to do is redeem her by removing the money from her sight and letting love come in through the servants' entrance, as it were.
'The servants' entrance' — that's a precise metaphor, Daniel.
Rokesmith as secretary is, economically speaking, someone who has entered the labour market — working for wages, in a domestic hierarchy.
And Bella, in choosing to love the secretary rather than waiting for the heir, is in theory choosing labour over capital.
Of course, it turns out they're the same man, so the choice was never real.
But the fantasy of the choice — that love might exist prior to and independent of money — is what the novel is selling, and selling hard.
And yet — and I insist on this — there is something the novel gives Harmon that I find genuinely moving, beyond the plot mechanics.
He walks through the city as a dead man.
He haunts the Boffin household, he visits the place where his body was pulled from the river.
And there's a kind of lightness that comes with it — a freedom from expectation that Dickens treats, I think, with real tenderness.
The great London novels are full of men hiding — in plain sight, in lodgings, in aliases.
But Harmon is the only one who gets to perform his own inquest, conclude his own verdict of death, and then decide — on his own terms — to live.
A man who conducts his own inquest and votes to acquit himself.
That image will stay with me.
What we've been circling, I think, is the novel's central wager: that identity can be voluntarily surrendered, tested, and — maybe — recovered with more integrity than it started with.
Whether the novel fully earns that wager — whether the resolution is triumph or evasion — that, it seems, depends on who you ask.
After the break, we're turning to the Thames itself — and to the question of what the river takes, and what it gives back.

segments.title: The Society Dickens Built: Institutions as Machines

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with one question: what does society actually do to people?
Not what it claims to do — not what its philanthropists and lawyers and schoolmasters say they are doing — but what it actually does.
I'm joined today by three people who have spent serious time with this novel and with the world it describes.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and Our Mutual Friend, he will tell you, is the most ruthless anatomy Dickens ever performed.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person in the room who knows precisely what it meant, in the 1860s, to be poor, to be in debt, to be dependent on a parish.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, a writer, and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — someone who comes to Dickens not through the academy but through the throat.
Our opening question is the one the novel itself never stops asking: when Dickens builds his fictional society, what are the institutions actually for?
The thing that strikes you, reading this novel with fresh eyes, is how comprehensively Dickens has mapped the system.
You have the Veneerings, who represent finance capital in its most naked, newly minted form — money so fresh it hasn't even acquired a biography yet.
You have the Wilfer household, the Lammles, the Podsnaps — each one a different stratum of the middle class in various stages of performing and protecting their position.
And then you have the dust mounds — the literal foundation of the whole novel's wealth — which is to say, you have waste.
Dickens is saying, with extraordinary precision, that the wealth of this society is built on what it throws away.
And what it throws away includes people — Gaffer Hexam working the river for corpses, Betty Higden fleeing the workhouse, Jenny Wren surviving on scraps.
Daniel is right to begin with the dust mounds, because that image has a very precise historical meaning that Dickens's contemporary readers would have felt viscerally.
The dust contractors of mid-Victorian London were genuinely among the wealthiest men in the city — fortunes built on sifting cinders, bone, and household refuse.
Old Harmon's fortune is not a gothic fantasy — it's a very sober account of how certain kinds of wealth actually accumulated.
Now, the institution I keep returning to in this novel is the law — specifically, the way the Harmon will functions as an instrument of control reaching from beyond the grave.
A dead man's caprice dictates who shall marry whom, who shall inherit, who shall be reduced to a servant in a house they should own.
This is not melodrama — in mid-Victorian England, testamentary power of that kind was absolutely real, and absolutely unbreakable.
What I love about the way Dickens sets all this up is the dinner party — those extraordinary early chapters with the Veneerings.
He gives you the whole of society reflected in that dining-room table — and the table itself is brand new, like everything the Veneerings possess.
There's a passage I return to again and again, where Dickens describes the Veneerings as having 'a bran-new house, a bran-new carriage, bran-new harness, bran-new furniture.'
'Everything about the Veneerings was spick and span new. All their furniture was new, all their friends were new, all their servants were new.'
That comic accumulation of 'new' — Dickens is doing two things at once there.
He's making you laugh, and he's making you slightly uneasy — because newness in this novel is not innocence, it's erasure.
Oliver's point about erasure goes to something I think is central to the novel's political argument.
The Veneerings have no history because capital in this phase doesn't want history — history would mean accountability, origins, the question of where the money came from.
Then look at Podsnap — who is in some ways the novel's most devastating portrait of an institution disguised as a man.
Podsnappery — Dickens actually coins the word — is a system for not knowing things that would be inconvenient to know.
The gesture Dickens gives him — sweeping uncomfortable facts off the table with a wave of the arm — is a perfect image of how ideology actually functions.
And Podsnap's daughter Georgiana is one of the quietest tragedies in the book — sacrificed on the altar of that ideology.
The Lammles target her precisely because her father's wealth and his public persona have rendered her invisible as a person — she is property, not a child.
Now, if we are talking about institutions as machines, I want to bring in the Poor Law — which is embodied in this novel in the figure of Betty Higden.
Betty Higden's terror of the workhouse is not sentimental decoration — it is a historically precise rendering of how the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act was experienced by working people.
The workhouse was designed, deliberately, to be worse than any alternative — that was not a failure of the system, it was the point of the system.
And Dickens understood that with a fury that never left him from Oliver Twist to this last great book.
Betty Higden is one of those characters where you feel the performance shift completely — she's not played for laughter at any point.
There's that extraordinary passage where she explains why she will die on the road rather than enter the workhouse — and Dickens lets her speak with a plain, exhausted dignity.
She says something to the effect that 'I have worked hard, worked honest, and I will not die a pauper's death in a pauper's place.'
The rhythm of that — the repetition of 'pauper's' — is Dickens the performer knowing exactly where the weight falls.
And when she dies, in the open air, having made it just far enough to not be taken by the institution she feared — that is the novel making its argument without a word of commentary.
That death is Dickens at his most radical — because he refuses to let it be private grief.
Betty Higden dies fleeing an institution that was created by an act of Parliament, administered by boards of guardians, funded by ratepayers, celebrated by economists.
Her death is a policy outcome — and Dickens knew it, and wanted the reader to know it.
This is why I argue the novel is more radical than anything Dickens's contemporaries gave him credit for.
He's not asking for kinder institutions — he's showing you institutions that are working exactly as designed, and finding that design monstrous.
I'd push back very gently on 'more radical than his contemporaries recognized' — because some of them recognized it quite clearly and were alarmed by it.
The Saturday Review, which was not a journal friendly to sentimentality or radicalism, found Our Mutual Friend troublingly hostile to the established order.
But I think the deeper point you're making, Daniel, stands — which is that Dickens doesn't offer a reform programme, he offers a diagnosis.
And the diagnosis is systemic, not individual — the villains are not wicked men ruining an otherwise healthy society, they are nodes in a network that produces wickedness.
Nodes in a network — I'd like to see Dickens use that phrase, though I suspect he'd have funnier words for it.
But that is exactly what the Veneering dinner table is — a diagram of the network, all those characters bouncing off each other like billiard balls.
Twemlow, poor dear Twemlow, perpetually confused about whether he is the Veneerings' oldest friend or newest — he is the novel's conscience dressed up as a mild-mannered gentleman.
And at the very end of the novel, Twemlow has his one great moment — he defends Eugene Wrayburn's marriage to Lizzie in that final dinner scene.
The mildest man in the book stands up to Podsnap and every other pompous voice in the room — and Dickens gives him the last word.
That's not sentiment — that's Dickens saying the only institution that works in this novel is the solitary human conscience.
The solitary human conscience — set against every institution the novel has spent eight hundred pages dissecting.
That is, as Oliver says, not sentiment — that is a structural argument about what survives when everything else is revealed as performance or exploitation.
In our next segment, we're going to look closely at the river — which in this novel is at once the novel's most powerful symbol and its most concrete economic fact.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Mutual Friends: The Novel's Faith in Love and Witness

utterances.text: We've spent this episode following the Thames through its darkest currents — money, death, and the machinery of class.
But Dickens didn't write this novel to leave us in the mud.
He wrote it as an act of faith — faith that love can persist, that witness matters, and that the human capacity for genuine feeling might outlast the worst the world throws at it.
So to close, I want to ask each of you — does the novel earn that faith?
Oliver, let's start with you — you've lived inside this prose more than most of us.
Does it earn its faith? Emphatically, yes — but not cheaply, and not without cost.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel — and I have returned to it many times — is that the love at its centre is forged through deception.
John Rokesmith — Harmon in disguise — watches Bella Wilfer without her knowing who he truly is.
And yet what he witnesses — her transformation from vain and mercenary to genuinely generous — is as honest a portrait of moral growth as Victorian fiction offers.
The moment she refuses the Boffin money — when she says she would rather be John Rokesmith's wife in poverty than the heiress to a fortune she hasn't earned — that scene undoes me every time.
Dickens lets her earn the happy ending by becoming worthy of it.
That is not sentimentality. That is craft.
I take the point about craft — and I don't want to be the voice that dismantles every happiness — but I think the more interesting question is: who does the novel let love rescue?
Because it is not everyone.
Jenny Wren and Lizzie Hexam and Riah — they witness love, they enable it, they are the novel's most morally clear-eyed figures.
But their own deliverance is partial at best. Jenny remains in poverty with her drunken father-child.
Lizzie gets Eugene — but Eugene is the man who pursued her in the most predatory terms imaginable before near-death remade him.
Dickens is honest enough that the novel's faith in love is not distributed evenly along class lines.
And yet — and this is what I find genuinely moving — he gives the lower-class characters the most dignity, the most moral authority.
Jenny Wren's rooftop vision — where she asks the sick and weary to 'come up and be dead' — is the closest the novel comes to genuine transcendence.
'Come up and be dead. Come up and be dead.'
That is a working-class child offering the world's only reliable relief from suffering — and Dickens treats it with absolute seriousness.
What Daniel is pointing to is, I think, one of the novel's most structurally interesting moves — the way it displaces moral authority onto those who have no legal authority whatsoever.
Jenny Wren has no rights at common law worth speaking of. Lizzie Hexam was the daughter of a man who robbed the dead.
Riah is legally excluded from most of the civil protections that others took for granted — and Dickens knew this.
And yet the novel repeatedly asks us to look at these figures — these witnesses — and see the truth of human experience that the respectable world is too busy or too afraid to acknowledge.
That is not a sentimental gesture. That is a philosophical position — and a fairly radical one for 1865.
The novel's faith in love is inseparable from its faith in the testimony of those the law ignores.
And then there is the remarkable fact that Eugene Wrayburn survives at all — that Dickens brought him back from the river's edge.
Because in an earlier draft he planned to kill him. He reconsidered.
What changes Eugene is not argument, not social pressure — it's Lizzie's love, and the near-death experience of the Thames itself.
The river — which the novel uses as a running image of death and money and corruption — becomes the site of rebirth.
And his deathbed proposal to Lizzie — 'in the name of what was romantic in us both' — is one of the great sentences.
'In the name of what was romantic in us both.'
He doesn't claim virtue. He doesn't pretend he was good. He appeals to something that survived both his worst self and the river's attempt to finish him.
And Mortimer Lightwood witnesses that scene. He's the friend who carries that broken body back to shore.
Mortimer is the novel's most underestimated character, I think.
He begins as a cynical, fashionable man, performing boredom for Society's approval.
By the end, his loyalty to Eugene — which costs him socially — is the novel's quiet argument that friendship is its own form of love.
The title is 'Our Mutual Friend' — not our shared property, not our common acquaintance — but a friend held in common, tended in common.
That mutuality — between people who would not naturally meet, between those the world would keep apart — is what Dickens is betting on.
I want to end on Mr Boffin — because his arc is the most misunderstood in the novel and also, I think, its most audacious act of faith.
Boffin performs the miser — convincingly enough that readers wrote to Dickens in genuine alarm.
He plays the role of corruption made flesh — in order to complete Bella's moral education.
And then, at the revelation, he reverts entirely to the Golden Dustman — warm, eccentric, luminously generous.
The reveal is the novel saying: the performance of wickedness does not make you wicked.
Character is not destroyed by contact with the worst of what money does — if the underlying goodness is real enough.
That strikes me as the right note on which to land — the Golden Dustman, rising from the heap.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that looks unflinchingly at everything money corrupts — bodies, language, love, even death itself.
And yet it refuses to concede that corruption is the whole story.
Dickens places his faith in witnesses — the small, the overlooked, the ones who work with their hands and dream from rooftops.
And he places his faith in the reader — which is, in the end, a form of mutual friendship.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and James Blackstone for a conversation worthy of the novel.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. We'll see you next time — from the river.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

c18:p1.text:
It was a school for all ages, and for both sexes. The latter were kept
      apart, and the former were partitioned off into square assortments. But,
      all the place was pervaded by a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil
      was childish and innocent. This pretence, much favoured by the
      lady-visitors, led to the ghastliest absurdities. Young women old in the
      vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves
      enthralled by the good child’s book, the Adventures of Little Margery, who
      resided in the village cottage by the mill; severely reproved and morally
      squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty; divided her
      porridge with singing birds; denied herself a new nankeen bonnet, on the
      ground that the turnips did not wear nankeen bonnets, neither did the
      sheep who ate them; who plaited straw and delivered the dreariest orations
      to all comers, at all sorts of unseasonable times. So, unwieldy young
      dredgers and hulking mudlarks were referred to the experiences of Thomas
      Twopence, who, having resolved not to rob (under circumstances of uncommon
      atrocity) his particular friend and benefactor, of eighteenpence,
      presently came into supernatural possession of three and sixpence, and
      lived a shining light ever afterwards. (Note, that the benefactor came to
      no good.) Several swaggering sinners had written their own biographies in
      the same strain; it always appearing from the lessons of those very
      boastful persons, that you were to do good, not because it  was  good, but
      because you were to make a good thing of it. Contrariwise, the adult
      pupils were taught to read (if they could learn) out of the New Testament;
      and by dint of stumbling over the syllables and keeping their bewildered
      eyes on the particular syllables coming round to their turn, were as
      absolutely ignorant of the sublime history, as if they had never seen or
      heard of it. An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a
      school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white,
      jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night. And particularly
      every Sunday night. For then, an inclined plane of unfortunate infants
      would be handed over to the prosiest and worst of all the teachers with
      good intentions, whom nobody older would endure. Who, taking his stand on
      the floor before them as chief executioner, would be attended by a
      conventional volunteer boy as executioner’s assistant. When and where it
      first became the conventional system that a weary or inattentive infant in
      a class must have its face smoothed downward with a hot hand, or when and
      where the conventional volunteer boy first beheld such system in
      operation, and became inflamed with a sacred zeal to administer it,
      matters not. It was the function of the chief executioner to hold forth,
      and it was the function of the acolyte to dart at sleeping infants,
      yawning infants, restless infants, whimpering infants, and smooth their
      wretched faces; sometimes with one hand, as if he were anointing them for
      a whisker; sometimes with both hands, applied after the fashion of
      blinkers. And so the jumble would be in action in this department for a
      mortal hour; the exponent drawling on to My Dearert Childerrenerr, let us
      say, for example, about the beautiful coming to the Sepulchre; and
      repeating the word Sepulchre (commonly used among infants) five hundred
      times, and never once hinting what it meant; the conventional boy
      smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole
      hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes,
      whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in
      High Market for the purpose.
c18:p1.summary: The narrator satirizes the school's pretense of innocence, the unsuitable moral literature forced on corrupt pupils, and the brutal Sunday school system where teachers violently 'smooth' inattentive children.
c18:p1.best_quote: An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.

On Friday the Ninth of June in the present year, Mr and Mrs Boffin (in
      their manuscript dress of receiving Mr and Mrs Lammle at breakfast) were
      on the South Eastern Railway with me, in a terribly destructive accident.
      When I had done what I could to help others, I climbed back into my
      carriage—nearly turned over a viaduct, and caught aslant upon the
      turn—to extricate the worthy couple. They were much soiled, but
      otherwise unhurt. The same happy result attended Miss Bella Wilfer on her
      wedding day, and Mr Riderhood inspecting Bradley Headstone’s red
      neckerchief as he lay asleep. I remember with devout thankfulness that I
      can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I
      was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with
      which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
c67:p61.summary: Dickens recounts his experience in the Staplehurst railway accident of June 9, 1865, expressing gratitude for his miraculous escape and reflecting on mortality in connection with the novel's conclusion.

c33:p48.text:
However, the great subject of the happiness of Mr and Mrs Lammle must not
      be allowed to vanish with the other vanishments—with the vanishing
      of the murderer, the vanishing of Julius Handford, the vanishing of Lizzie
      Hexam,—and therefore Veneering must recall the present sheep to the
      pen from which they have strayed. Who so fit to discourse of the happiness
      of Mr and Mrs Lammle, they being the dearest and oldest friends he has in
      the world; or what audience so fit for him to take into his confidence as
      that audience, a noun of multitude or signifying many, who are all the
      oldest and dearest friends he has in the world? So Veneering, without the
      formality of rising, launches into a familiar oration, gradually toning
      into the Parliamentary sing-song, in which he sees at that board his dear
      friend Twemlow who on that day twelvemonth bestowed on his dear friend
      Lammle the fair hand of his dear friend Sophronia, and in which he also
      sees at that board his dear friends Boots and Brewer whose rallying round
      him at a period when his dear friend Lady Tippins likewise rallied round
      him—ay, and in the foremost rank—he can never forget while
      memory holds her seat. But he is free to confess that he misses from that
      board his dear old friend Podsnap, though he is well represented by his
      dear young friend Georgiana. And he further sees at that board (this he
      announces with pomp, as if exulting in the powers of an extraordinary
      telescope) his friend Mr Fledgeby, if he will permit him to call him so.
      For all of these reasons, and many more which he right well knows will
      have occurred to persons of your exceptional acuteness, he is here to
      submit to you that the time has arrived when, with our hearts in our
      glasses, with tears in our eyes, with blessings on our lips, and in a
      general way with a profusion of gammon and spinach in our emotional
      larders, we should one and all drink to our dear friends the Lammles,
      wishing them many years as happy as the last, and many many friends as
      congenially united as themselves. And this he will add; that Anastatia
      Veneering (who is instantly heard to weep) is formed on the same model as
      her old and chosen friend Sophronia Lammle, in respect that she is devoted
      to the man who wooed and won her, and nobly discharges the duties of a
      wife.
c33:p48.summary: Veneering delivers an extended, self-congratulatory oration celebrating the Lammles' marriage and the assembled company's friendship, filled with parliamentary bombast and hypocritical sentiment.

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.
c67:p60.best_quote: I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.

c2:p3.text:
But, it was not this which steeped the feeble soul of Twemlow in
      confusion. This he was used to, and could take soundings of. The abyss to
      which he could find no bottom, and from which started forth the engrossing
      and ever-swelling difficulty of his life, was the insoluble question
      whether he was Veneering’s oldest friend, or newest friend. To the
      excogitation of this problem, the harmless gentleman had devoted many
      anxious hours, both in his lodgings over the livery stable-yard, and in
      the cold gloom, favourable to meditation, of Saint James’s Square. Thus.
      Twemlow had first known Veneering at his club, where Veneering then knew
      nobody but the man who made them known to one another, who seemed to be
      the most intimate friend he had in the world, and whom he had known two
      days—the bond of union between their souls, the nefarious conduct of
      the committee respecting the cookery of a fillet of veal, having been
      accidentally cemented at that date. Immediately upon this, Twemlow
      received an invitation to dine with Veneering, and dined: the man being of
      the party. Immediately upon that, Twemlow received an invitation to dine
      with the man, and dined: Veneering being of the party. At the man’s were a
      Member, an Engineer, a Payer-off of the National Debt, a Poem on
      Shakespeare, a Grievance, and a Public Office, who all seem to be utter
      strangers to Veneering. And yet immediately after that, Twemlow received
      an invitation to dine at Veneerings, expressly to meet the Member, the
      Engineer, the Payer-off of the National Debt, the Poem on Shakespeare, the
      Grievance, and the Public Office, and, dining, discovered that all of them
      were the most intimate friends Veneering had in the world, and that the
      wives of all of them (who were all there) were the objects of Mrs
      Veneering’s most devoted affection and tender confidence.
